Debt Crisis Hammers Mexico’s Transportation Equipment Sector, Thousands of Jobs at Risk

A sudden debt crisis has struck Mexico’s transportation equipment industry, leaving dozens of firms struggling to stay afloat and putting thousands of jobs and production sites in jeopardy. The ongoing turmoil began last month when a group of mid-sized manufacturers announced they could not meet upcoming bond payments, triggering a wave of credit downgrades and a tightening of financing conditions across the sector.

In the city of Saltillo, a regional hub for transportation equipment production, the effects are already being felt. At the sprawling plant of Equipos Moviles del Norte, operations manager Luis Ríos described the situation as “the most severe financial challenge in decades.” He explained that suppliers of raw materials and components have begun demanding upfront payment, a shift that has strained already thin cash reserves. “We’re doing everything possible to keep the lines running, but our credit lines have been frozen. Our workers are anxious, and we’re having frank conversations about short-term furloughs if conditions do not improve.”

Union leaders are warning of looming layoffs. Maricela Guzmán, general secretary of the Sindicato de Trabajadores del Transporte Industrial, said, “Our members are worried. Some factories have already reduced shifts or suspended overtime. We’re urging employers to protect jobs, but the financial pressure is enormous.”

According to the Cámara Nacional de Equipos de Transporte, at least 18 firms have entered restructuring proceedings since the start of June. Industry analysts estimate that more than 7,000 jobs have been directly affected by shift reductions, temporary plant closures, or wage delays in states such as Nuevo León, Coahuila, and Querétaro.

“The entire sector is facing a liquidity squeeze,” said consultant Rodrigo Valdez, who has monitored the industry for over a decade. “A large portion of transportation equipment firms relied on rolling short-term debt to finance operations. With lenders pulling back, companies are being forced to sell assets or halt investment plans. We could see a wave of consolidations or bankruptcies if the credit freeze continues.”

The crisis has also halted expansion projects. In San Luis Potosí, construction of a new assembly site by Montajes Ferroviarios Centro has been paused indefinitely, according to local officials. “We had hoped to create 500 new jobs, but until financial conditions stabilize, everything is on hold,” said company spokesperson Diana Morales.

Industry leaders are now calling on authorities to facilitate emergency credit lines and ensure continued operations. As of today, uncertainty remains high, with no clear resolution in sight and the fate of thousands of workers hanging in the balance.
